title: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 23-29 (Nag Hammadi Codex II, pages 38-39)
source: Nag Hammadi Codex II page photographs (Claremont Colleges Digital Library, Nag Hammadi Archive) + Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley (CC BY 4.0) + English by Mark M. Mattison (public domain)
description: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 23-29, in the Coptic of Nag Hammadi Codex II, pages 38-39, with each saying linked to the photograph of the papyrus page and an English translation.
introduction:
The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, introduced as the hidden sayings written down by Didymos Judas Thomas. The only complete copy is the second tractate of Nag Hammadi Codex II, a papyrus book in Coptic copied in the 4th century and found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945; it is now in the Coptic Museum, Cairo (inv. 10544). Greek fragments of the work survive in three Oxyrhynchus papyri (P. Oxy. 1, 654 and 655), which are not shown here.

This entry covers the sayings 23-29, which begin on codex page 38; the end of saying 29 is on page 39. The Coptic is given line by line; the small numbers are codex page and line (for example 33.5), so each line can be found on the photograph. Page and line breaks follow the Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley, which he made from the photographs of The Facsimile Edition of the Nag Hammadi Codices, the negatives shown here.

Photograph: Codex II page 38, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 48, CCDL nha 2881; Nag Hammadi Archive of the Institute for Antiquity and Christianity, Claremont Colleges Digital Library. Checked on the photograph: page 38 line 1 begins 'ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉϯⲛⲁⲥⲉⲧⲡⲧⲏⲛⲉ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ' and line 34 reads 'ⲛ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ ⲡⲉ ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ⳿ ϯⲣ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ' (the beginning of the last line is damaged).
translator_notes: Coptic: Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition (Paul C. Dilley), version 6.2.0, CC BY 4.0, shown in the manuscript's own spelling with words grouped as bound groups. Editorial signs are the edition's: square brackets mark letters lost in a gap (restored by the editor, or dots for the number of lost letters), a dot under a letter marks an uncertain reading, round brackets write out a letter abbreviated by a stroke at a line end, angle brackets mark letters added by the editor, curly brackets letters the editor removes, double square brackets letters erased by the scribe.

The small numbers in the Coptic are codex page and line (page.line) as marked in the edition. Where a word is divided between two lines on the papyrus, the edition sometimes keeps the word whole on one line, so a line can begin a few letters earlier or later on the photograph (for example 39.33-34, and the page change inside saying 13).

English: Mark M. Mattison, The Gospel of Thomas (public domain). Mattison's symbols: [ ] gap in the text, ( ) editorial insertion, / \ editorial correction of a scribal error. The saying headings are his.

translation.text:
His disciples said, "Show us the place where you are, because we need to look for it."

He said to them, "Anyone who has ears to hear should hear! Light exists within a person of light, and they light up the whole world. If they don't shine, there's darkness."

38.31ⲙⲉⲧⲁⲛⲟⲉⲓ
translation.text: Jesus said, "I stood in the middle of the world and appeared to them in the flesh. I found them all drunk; I didn't find any of them thirsty. My soul ached for the children of humanity, because they were blind in their hearts and couldn't see. They came into the world empty and plan on leaving the world empty. Meanwhile, they're drunk. When they shake off their wine, then they'll change."
translation.scan_note: On page 38 lines 20-31 (Codex II page 38, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 48, CCDL nha 2881). Opens 'ⲡⲉϫⲉ' at 38.20; ends 'ⲙⲉⲧⲁⲛⲟⲉⲓ' at 38.31. translation.text: Jesus said, "If the flesh came into existence because of spirit, that's amazing. If spirit came into existence because of the body, that's really amazing! But I'm amazed at how [such] great wealth has been placed in this poverty."
